pumac-2016-power-01.title: Answers
pumac-2016-power-01.body:
(a) Yes: $2\le2\cdot1$ ($c=2$, $N=0$). (b) Yes: $2\le n$ for $n\ge2$ ($c=1,N=2$). (c) No: for any $c$, $n>2c$ once $n$ is large.
(d) Yes: we show $n^3\le2^n$ for all $n\ge10$ (so $c=1$, $N=10$). For $n=10$: $1000\le1024$. If $n^3\le2^n$ for some $n\ge10$, then $(n+1)^3=n^3(1+\frac1n)^3\le n^3(1.1)^3<2n^3\le2^{n+1}$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2016-power-02.title: Constants
pumac-2016-power-02.body: Take $c_1,N_1$ with $f\le c_1g$ for $n\ge N_1$ and $c_2,N_2$ with $g\le c_2h$ for $n\ge N_2$. For $n\ge N=\max(N_1,N_2)$, $f(n)\le c_1g(n)\le c_1c_2h(n)$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2016-power-03.title: Answers
pumac-2016-power-03.body:
(a) Yes ($f\le3n^2$, $k=2$). (b) No: $\sqrt n/2\le f(n)$ grows faster than $(\lg n)^k$ for every $k$ (as $\lg n\le\log_2 n+1$ and $n^{1/(2k)}/\log_2n\to\infty$). (c) No: $n!\ge(n/2)^{n/2}$ eventually exceeds $cn^k$.
(d) No: for any $k$ and $c$, if $n\ge2^{k+1}$ then $\lg n=\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\ge k+1$ so $n^{\lg n}\ge n^{k+1}=n\cdot n^k>c\,n^k$ as soon as $n>c$. So $n^{\lg n}\ne O(n^k)$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2016-power-04.title: Constants and exponents
pumac-2016-power-04.body:
Let $f\le c_1h^{k_1}$ for $n\ge N_1$ and $g\le c_2h^{k_2}$ for $n\ge N_2$. Put $N=\max(N_1,N_2)$.
(a) With $k=\max(k_1,k_2)$ and $h\ge1$ (for $h(n)\ge1$; if $h=0$ at some $n$ only finitely many $n$ matter), $f+g\le(c_1+c_2)h^k$ for $n\ge N$. (b) $fg\le c_1c_2h^{k_1+k_2}$ for $n\ge N$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2016-power-05.title: Answers
pumac-2016-power-05.body: (a) No: for $k=2$, $n^k|f(n)|=1\not<1$ for every $n$. (b) Yes: $2^n>n^{k+1}$ for large $n$, so $n^k/2^n<1/n<1$. (c) Yes: given $k$, for $n\ge2^k$ we have $\lg n=\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\ge k+1$, so $n^k/n^{\lg n}\le n^{-1}<1$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2016-power-06.title: Epsilon management
pumac-2016-power-06.body:
(a) Given $k$, choose $N$ so large that for $n\ge N$: $n^{k+1}|f(n)|<1$, $n^{k+1}|g(n)|<1$ and $n\ge2$. Then $n^k|f+g|\le n^k|f|+n^k|g|<\frac2n\le1$.
(b) Given $k$, for $n$ large $n^k|f|<1$ and $n^k|g|<1$; hence $n^k|fg|\le n^k|f|\cdot n^k|g|<1$ (for $n\ge1$, $n^k\le n^{2k}$). $\blacksquare$

pumac-2016-power-07.title: Absorb the polynomial
pumac-2016-power-07.body: Let $f(n)\le cn^{k_0}$ for $n\ge N_0$; absorbing $c$ (taking $n\ge c$) assume $f(n)\le n^{k_0+1}$. Given $k$, choose $N$ such that $n^{k+k_0+1}|g(n)|<1$ for $n\ge N$ and $N\ge N_0$. Then $n^k|f(n)g(n)|\le n^{k+k_0+1}|g(n)|<1$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2016-power-08.title: Answers
pumac-2016-power-08.body: (a) The algorithm performs at least $n$ additions on input $n$. If it were polynomial-time, then $n\le c(\lg n)^k$ for all large $n$; but $n/(\lg n)^k\to\infty$ (the length $\lg n\approx\log_2n$ is exponentially smaller than $n$). (b) Multiply $n$ by $n+1$ and divide by $2$ (a shift): schoolbook multiplication takes $O((\lg n)^2)$ operations. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2016-power-09.title: Answers
pumac-2016-power-09.body: (a) True: $\Pr=\frac{4+3+2+1}{36}=\frac{10}{36}<\frac12$. (b) False: if the first roll is $6$, the sum is $\ge9$ iff the second roll is $\ge3$, probability $\frac46>\frac12$ (the first roll $5$ also fails: $\frac36$ is not $<\frac12$; $6$ is the clear counterexample). (c) True: if the first roll is $1$, the sum is at most $7$, so the probability is $0<\frac12$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2016-power-10.title: Proofs
pumac-2016-power-10.body:
(a) For $i
e j$ sum the product formula over all values of the other variables: $\Pr[X_i=x_i,X_j=x_j]=\sum_{	ext{others}}\prod_t\Pr[X_t=x_t]=\Pr[X_i=x_i]\Pr[X_j=x_j]\prod_{t
e i,j}\sum_{x_t}\Pr[X_t=x_t]=\Pr[X_i=x_i]\Pr[X_j=x_j]$.
(b) Each $X_i$ is a fair bit, and for each pair, e.g. $(X_1,X_2)$, the four strings give the four pairs $(0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)$ once each: probability $ rac14= rac12\cdot rac12$. So they are pairwise independent. They are not independent: $\Pr[X_1=X_2=X_3=0]=\Pr[w=000]= rac14
e rac18$. $ lacksquare$

pumac-2016-power-12.title: Expand the square
pumac-2016-power-12.body:
Put $\mu_i=E(X_i)$, $Y_i=X_i-\mu_i$ (pairwise independent, mean $0$). By linearity of expectation $E(\sum X_i)=\sum\mu_i$, so
$$V\Bigl(\sum X_i\Bigr)=E\Bigl(\bigl(\sum Y_i\bigr)^2\Bigr)=\sum_iE(Y_i^2)+\sum_{i\ne j}E(Y_iY_j).$$
For $i\ne j$, by independence $E(Y_iY_j)=\sum_{a,b}ab\Pr[Y_i=a,Y_j=b]=\sum_aa\Pr[Y_i=a]\sum_bb\Pr[Y_j=b]=E(Y_i)E(Y_j)=0$. Hence $V(\sum X_i)=\sum E(Y_i^2)=\sum V(X_i)$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2016-power-13.title: Proof
pumac-2016-power-13.body: $|X-E(X)|\ge t$ iff $(X-E(X))^2\ge t^2$, and $(X-E(X))^2\ge0$. By Markov's inequality, $\Pr[(X-E(X))^2\ge t^2]\le E((X-E(X))^2)/t^2=V(X)/t^2$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2016-power-14.title: Both bounds
pumac-2016-power-14.body: Let $X$ be the number of heads; $E(X)=500$. (a) Markov: $\Pr[X\ge600]\le\frac{500}{600}=\frac56$. (b) The flips are independent, so $V(X)=1000\cdot\frac14=250$ (by Problem 3.4). Chebyshev: $\Pr[|X-500|\ge100]\le\frac{250}{100^2}=\frac1{40}$; by symmetry of the distribution about $500$ the event $X\ge600$ has half of this probability: $\Pr[X\ge600]\le\frac1{80}$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2016-power-15.title: Answers
pumac-2016-power-15.body: (a) M,A,T,H $\to$ W,K,D,R: **WKDR**. (b) Shift back by $8$: X,C,U,I,K $\to$ P,U,M,A,C: **PUMAC**. (c) Try shifts: shifting every letter back by $23$ (equivalently forward by $3$) gives **INTEGRATIONBYSMARTS** ("Integration by Smarts"), so the shift was $23$ ($I+23\equiv F$). $\blacksquare$

pumac-2016-power-17.title: Answers
pumac-2016-power-17.body: (a) $x\oplus x=0$ (the all-zero string). (b) $x\oplus0=x$. (c) Yes: bitwise $b_1\oplus b_2=b_2\oplus b_1$. (d) Yes: the $i$-th bit of both sides is $1$ iff an odd number of the $i$-th bits of $x,y,z$ are $1$. (e) $x\oplus z=x\oplus(x\oplus y)=(x\oplus x)\oplus y=0\oplus y=y$ (by (d),(a),(b)). (f) If $y=z$ clearly $x\oplus y=x\oplus z$. Conversely if $x\oplus y=x\oplus z$, xor both sides with $x$: $y=(x\oplus x)\oplus y=x\oplus(x\oplus y)=x\oplus(x\oplus z)=z$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2016-power-18.title: Decrypt
pumac-2016-power-18.body: Bob computes $c\oplus k=(m\oplus k)\oplus k=m\oplus(k\oplus k)=m\oplus0=m$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2016-power-19.title: Description
pumac-2016-power-19.body: Key space $K_n=\{0,1\}^n$ and ciphertext space $C_n=\{0,1\}^n$. $G(1^n)$ outputs $n$ independent uniformly random bits $k$ (a PPT algorithm). $E_k(m)=m\oplus k$ and $D_k(c)=c\oplus k$; both are deterministic and polynomial-time, and $D_k(E_k(m))=m$ by Problem 4.4. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2016-power-20.title: Check Definition 4.1.1
pumac-2016-power-20.body: An encryption scheme needs a decryption algorithm $D$ with $D_k(E_k(m))=m$ for every message $m$. If $E_k(m)=0$ for all $m$, then $D_k(0)$ would have to equal every message simultaneously, which is impossible once there are two different messages. So that $E$ is not part of any valid encryption scheme (a valid $E_k$ must be injective). $\blacksquare$

pumac-2016-power-21.title: Both directions
pumac-2016-power-21.body:
For an adversary that, for the messages $m_0,m_1$ it picks, outputs $b'=A(c)$ on ciphertext $c$, write $p_b=\Pr[A(E_k(m_b))=1]$. Its success probability is $\frac12(1-p_0)+\frac12p_1=\frac12+\frac12(p_1-p_0)$. $(\ast)$

**(indist. $\Rightarrow$ guessing).** Let neg be the negligible function of the first definition and $A'$ a PPT guessing adversary. For each pair $(m_0,m_1)$ that $A'$ may pick, the algorithm $A(c)$ = (the guess of $A'$ on $c$ with the pair $(m_0,m_1)$ fixed) is PPT, so $|p_1-p_0|\le\mathrm{neg}(n)$. By $(\ast)$, given that pair, $A'$ wins with probability $\le\frac12+\frac12\mathrm{neg}(n)$; averaging over $A'$'s choice of pair, $A'$ wins with probability $\le\frac12+\mathrm{neg}(n)$.

**(guessing $\Rightarrow$ indist.).** Let neg$'$ be the negligible function of the second definition. Let $n,m_0,m_1$ and a PPT $A$ be given. Define the guessing adversary $A'$ which picks $m_0,m_1$ and outputs $A(c)$ if $p_1\ge p_0$, and $1-A(c)$ otherwise (this choice only depends on the fixed $n,m_0,m_1,A$). By $(\ast)$ it wins with probability $\frac12+\frac12|p_1-p_0|\le\frac12+\mathrm{neg}'(n)$, so $|p_1-p_0|\le2\,\mathrm{neg}'(n)$, which is negligible. So the first definition holds with $2\,\mathrm{neg}'$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2016-power-22.title: Bijection of keys
pumac-2016-power-22.body:
Fix $n$, messages $m_0,m_1$ and any algorithm $A$ (even unbounded). Let $d=m_0\oplus m_1$. The map $k\mapsto k'=k\oplus d$ is a bijection of $\{0,1\}^n$ and $m_0\oplus k=m_1\oplus k'$. Hence
$$\Pr[A(m_0\oplus k)=1]=\frac1{2^n}\sum_k\Pr[A(m_1\oplus(k\oplus d))=1]=\frac1{2^n}\sum_{k'}\Pr[A(m_1\oplus k')=1]=\Pr[A(m_1\oplus k)=1].$$
The difference is $0$, which is below any negligible function. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2016-power-23.title: Attack
pumac-2016-power-23.body:
(a) Let $A$ split the ciphertext into $n$ chunks $c_1,\dots,c_n$ and output $1$ iff $c_1=\dots=c_n$. For $m_0=0^{8n}$ all chunks equal $k$, so $A$ outputs $1$ with probability $1$. For $m_1=0^{8n-1}1$ the last chunk is $0000000\,1\oplus k\ne k$, so $A$ outputs $0$ with probability $1$. The difference is $1$ for every $n>1$, not negligible: insecure.
(b) Reusing a key on several blocks (or messages) is the same situation: the repetition of the key leaks relations between plaintexts (e.g. $c_i\oplus c_j=m_i\oplus m_j$), and the same style of attack distinguishes messages. The one-time pad is secure only if each key bit is used once. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2016-power-24.title: Distinguishers
pumac-2016-power-24.body:
(a) $D$ outputs $1$ iff the last bit is $0$. On $H(x)$ it outputs $1$ always; on $U_{n+1}$ with probability $\frac12$. Difference $\frac12$: not negligible.
(b) $D$ outputs $1$ iff the first half equals the second half. On $H(x)$: always $1$; on $U_{2n}$: probability $2^{-n}$. Difference $1-2^{-n}$: not negligible.
(c) $|H(x)|=|x|$, so $\ell(n)=n\not>n$: $H$ does not stretch, hence is not a PRG.
(d) $|H(x)|=n+1$. $D$ outputs $1$ iff the xor of all bits except the first is $0$. For $H(x)$ this xor is $(x_1\oplus x_2)\oplus(x_2\oplus x_3)\oplus\dots\oplus(x_{n-1}\oplus x_n)\oplus(x_n\oplus x_1)=0$ (each $x_i$ appears twice), so $D$ outputs $1$ always; on $U_{n+1}$ the xor is $0$ with probability $\frac12$. Difference $\frac12$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2016-power-25.title: Reduction to the PRG property
pumac-2016-power-25.body:
**Valid scheme.** $G$ is PPT, $E_k,D_k$ are deterministic polynomial-time ($H$ is polynomial-time and $\ell(n)$ is polynomial in $n$), and $D_k(E_k(m))=(m\oplus H(k))\oplus H(k)=m$.

**Security.** Suppose some PPT $A$ and messages $m_0,m_1$ have $|\Pr[A(m_0\oplus H(U_n))=1]-\Pr[A(m_1\oplus H(U_n))=1]|=\epsilon(n)$. Define $D(y)$: output $A(m_0\oplus y)$, and $D'(y)$: output $A(m_1\oplus y)$; both are PPT. For uniform $y=U_{\ell(n)}$, $m_0\oplus y$ and $m_1\oplus y$ are both uniform, so $\Pr[D(U_{\ell(n)})=1]=\Pr[D'(U_{\ell(n)})=1]$. By the triangle inequality,
$$\epsilon(n)\le\bigl|\Pr[D(H(U_n))=1]-\Pr[D(U_{\ell(n)})=1]\bigr|+\bigl|\Pr[D'(U_{\ell(n)})=1]-\Pr[D'(H(U_n))=1]\bigr|,$$
so $D$ or $D'$ distinguishes $H(U_n)$ from $U_{\ell(n)}$ with advantage $\ge\epsilon(n)/2$. Since $H$ is a PRG, that advantage is $<\mathrm{neg}(n)$, hence $\epsilon(n)<2\,\mathrm{neg}(n)$ is negligible. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2016-power-26.title: Inverters
pumac-2016-power-26.body:
(a) Given $s=f(x)$ and $1^n$, output $1^s0^{n-s}$; its bit sum is $s$, so $f(A(f(x),1^n))=f(x)$ always.
(b) Given $y=x^2$, compute the integer square root $\lfloor\sqrt y\rfloor=x$ by binary search on the bits of $x$ (try each next bit: it is $1$ iff the square of the candidate with that bit set is $\le y$); this takes polynomially many steps in the bit length. Then $f(x)=y$.
(c) Given $(p,t)$ with $t=k^{-1}$, compute $k'=t^{-1}\bmod p$ with the extended Euclidean algorithm in time polynomial in $\lg p$; then $(p,k')$ satisfies $f(p,k')=(p,(t^{-1})^{-1})=(p,t)$. So $A$ always succeeds. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2016-power-27a.title: Reduction
pumac-2016-power-27a.body: $g$ is polynomial-time computable. Suppose a PPT $A$ inverts $g$ on inputs of length $2n$ with probability $>\mathrm{neg}(2n)$ for some negligible $\mathrm{neg}$. Define $A'$ on input $(t,1^n)$: pick a random $y\in\{0,1\}^n$, run $A$ on $t\circ y$, and output the first $n$ bits of the result. If $t=f(x)$ with $x$ uniform, then $t\circ y=g(x\circ y)$ for a uniform $2n$-bit string $x\circ y$, so with probability $>\mathrm{neg}(2n)$ the output $(x',y')$ satisfies $f(x')\circ y'=f(x)\circ y$, i.e. $f(x')=f(x)$. So $A'$ inverts $f$ with probability $>\mathrm{neg}(2n)$. Since $n\mapsto\mathrm{neg}(2n)$ is again negligible (the class of negligible functions is closed under this substitution: $n^k\mathrm{neg}(2n)\le(2n)^k\mathrm{neg}(2n)\to0$), this contradicts that $f$ is one-way. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2016-power-27b.title: Chebyshev
pumac-2016-power-27b.body: Let $\bar X=\frac1m\sum X_i$, $E(\bar X)=\mu$. Each $X_i$ has variance $\mu(1-\mu)^2+(1-\mu)\mu^2=\mu(1-\mu)$; by pairwise independence variances add: $V(\bar X)=\frac1{m^2}\cdot m\mu(1-\mu)=\frac{\mu(1-\mu)}m$. Chebyshev gives $\Pr[|\bar X-\mu|\ge\epsilon]\le\frac{\mu(1-\mu)}{m\epsilon^2}$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2016-power-27c.title: Linearity
pumac-2016-power-27c.body: For fixed $x$, $y\mapsto b(x,y)=\bigoplus x_ky_k$ is additive: $b(x,y\oplus y')=b(x,y)\oplus b(x,y')$. If $A$ is always right, $g_j=b(x,r_j)\oplus b(x,e_i\oplus r_j)=b(x,r_j\oplus e_i\oplus r_j)=b(x,e_i)=x_i$ for every $j$. So the majority is $t_i=x_i$ for every $i$, and $B$ outputs $x$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2016-power-27d.title: Many good $x$, then majority
pumac-2016-power-27d.body:
**Size of $S$.** If $|S|<2^n\epsilon/2$, then the overall success probability is at most $\Pr[x\in S]\cdot1+\Pr[x\notin S]\bigl(\frac12+\frac\epsilon2\bigr)<\frac\epsilon2+\frac12+\frac\epsilon2=\frac12+\epsilon$, a contradiction.

**Majority.** Let $x\in S$ and fix $i$. Let $Y_j=1$ if $g_j=x_i$. Since $g_j=b(x,r_j)\oplus A(f(x),e_i\oplus r_j)$ and $e_i\oplus r_j$ is uniform, $g_j=x_i$ iff $A(f(x),e_i\oplus r_j)=b(x,e_i\oplus r_j)$, so $\Pr[Y_j=1]=\mu>\frac12+\frac\epsilon2$. The $Y_j$ are pairwise independent (the $r_j$ are, and the coins of $A$ are independent for different $j$). The majority is wrong only if $\frac1m\sum Y_j\le\frac12$, which requires $|\frac1m\sum Y_j-\mu|\ge\mu-\frac12\ge\frac\epsilon2$. By (b), this has probability at most $\frac{\mu(1-\mu)}{m(\epsilon/2)^2}\le\frac{1/4}{m\epsilon^2/4}=\frac1{m\epsilon^2}\le\frac1{2n}$. A union bound over the $n$ coordinates gives total failure probability $\le\frac12$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2016-power-27e.title: Pairwise independence from few random strings
pumac-2016-power-27e.body:
Let $\ell=\lceil\lg m\rceil$-ish with $2^\ell-1\ge m$ (take $\ell=\lceil\log_2(m+1)\rceil$; then $2^\ell\le2(m+1)$). $B$ picks independent uniform strings $s_1,\dots,s_\ell\in\{0,1\}^n$, and for each nonempty subset $T_j\subseteq\{1,\dots,\ell\}$ ($j=1,\dots,m$, distinct subsets) sets $r_j=\bigoplus_{l\in T_j}s_l$.

*Pairwise independence.* Let $T_1\ne T_2$ be two of the subsets with $r_1=\bigoplus_{T_1}s_l$, $r_2=\bigoplus_{T_2}s_l$. If neither contains the other, pick $l_1\in T_1\setminus T_2$ and $l_2\in T_2\setminus T_1$: given all other strings, $r_1$ is shifted by the uniform $s_{l_1}$ and $r_2$ by the independent uniform $s_{l_2}$, so $(r_1,r_2)$ is uniform on pairs. If (say) $T_2\subsetneq T_1$, pick $l_1\in T_1\setminus T_2$: $r_2$ does not involve $s_{l_1}$ and is uniform (as $T_2\ne\emptyset$), while $r_1=r_2\oplus\bigoplus_{T_1\setminus T_2}s_l$ is shifted by the uniform $s_{l_1}$: again $(r_1,r_2)$ is uniform. In all cases $\Pr[r_1=z_1,r_2=z_2]=4^{-n}$.

*Guessing the bits.* $B$ guesses uniformly random bits $b'_1,\dots,b'_\ell$. With probability $2^{-\ell}\ge\frac1{2(m+1)}\ge\frac1{4m}$ all guesses equal $b(x,s_l)$. Then, by linearity of $b(x,\cdot)$, defining $b_j=\bigoplus_{l\in T_j}b'_l$ gives $b_j=b(x,r_j)$ for all $j$, exactly the "magic" values. So, conditioned on the correct guess (probability $\ge\frac1{4m}$), $B$ behaves as in (d). $\blacksquare$

pumac-2016-power-27f.title: Putting it together
pumac-2016-power-27f.body: Take $m=\lceil2n/\epsilon^2\rceil$ (so that (d) applies; $\epsilon=\epsilon(n)$ is a non-negligible function with $1/\epsilon$ polynomially bounded for infinitely many $n$, so $m$ is polynomial in $n$ for those $n$). $B$ runs in time polynomial in $n$ and $m$: it samples $\ell=O(\lg m)$ strings, forms $m$ xors, and runs $A$ on $mn$ inputs. With probability $\ge\Pr[x\in S]\ge\frac\epsilon2$, $x\in S$; given $x\in S$, the guesses are right with probability $\ge\frac1{4m}$, and then $B$ returns $x$ with probability $\ge\frac12$. So $B$ inverts $f$ with probability at least $\frac\epsilon2\cdot\frac1{4m}\cdot\frac12=\frac{\epsilon}{16m}\ge\frac{\epsilon^3}{48n}$ (using $m\le3n/\epsilon^2$), which is non-negligible. This contradicts that $f$ is one-way. Hence no such $A$ exists, i.e. $b$ is a hard-core bit of $g$, and $g$ is one-way by (a). $\blacksquare$

pumac-2016-power-28.title: Bijectivity
pumac-2016-power-28.body: $g$ maps $\{0,1\}^{2n}$ into $\{0,1\}^{2n}$ (as $|f(x)|=|x|$). If $g(x_1\circ y_1)=g(x_2\circ y_2)$ then $f(x_1)=f(x_2)$ and $y_1=y_2$; $f$ is injective so $x_1=x_2$. So $g$ is injective on a finite set mapping to a set of the same size: bijective. By Theorem 7.3.2 $g$ is one-way, hence a one-way permutation, with the hard-core bit $b$. So when $f$ is a one-way permutation the theorem's conclusion ("$g$ is a one-way function with hard-core bit $b$") can be strengthened to "$g$ is a one-way permutation with hard-core bit $b$". $\blacksquare$

pumac-2016-power-29.title: From a distinguisher to a predictor
pumac-2016-power-29.body:
$H$ is polynomial-time and $|H(x)|=n+1>n$. Suppose a PPT $D$ has $|\Pr[D(f(x)\circ b(x))=1]-\Pr[D(U_{n+1})=1]|\ge\epsilon(n)$ ($x=U_n$) with $\epsilon$ non-negligible. Since $f$ is a permutation, $f(x)$ is uniform on $\{0,1\}^n$, so $U_{n+1}\sim f(x)\circ U_1$ and
$$\Pr[D(U_{n+1})=1]=\tfrac12\Pr[D(f(x)\circ b(x))=1]+\tfrac12\Pr[D(f(x)\circ\overline{b(x)})=1].$$
Hence $|\Pr[D(f(x)\circ b(x))=1]-\Pr[D(f(x)\circ\overline{b(x)})=1]|\ge2\epsilon$. Say (else flip the output of $D$) $\Pr[D(f(x)\circ b)=1]-\Pr[D(f(x)\circ\bar b)=1]\ge2\epsilon$. Define $A(f(x))$: choose a uniform bit $c$, compute $D(f(x)\circ c)$ and output $c$ if $D$ outputs $1$ and $\bar c$ otherwise. Then
$$\Pr[A=b(x)]=\tfrac12\Pr[D(f(x)\circ b(x))=1]+\tfrac12\Pr[D(f(x)\circ\overline{b(x)})=0]=\tfrac12+\tfrac12\bigl(\Pr[D(f\circ b)=1]-\Pr[D(f\circ\bar b)=1]\bigr)\ge\tfrac12+\epsilon,$$
contradicting that $b$ is hard-core. So $H$ is a PRG with $\ell(n)=n+1$.

**Existence.** If a one-way permutation $f$ exists, then by Theorem 7.3.2 and Problem 7.3, $g(x\circ y)=f(x)\circ y$ is a one-way permutation (defined on even lengths) with hard-core bit $b$; by the above, $H(x\circ y)=g(x\circ y)\circ b(x,y)$ is a PRG (on even input lengths, the same caveat as for $g$). $\blacksquare$

pumac-2016-power-30.title: Hybrids
pumac-2016-power-30.body:
For a function $\Gamma$ let $\varepsilon_\Gamma(n)=\sup_D|\Pr[D(\Gamma(U_n))=1]-\Pr[D(U_{|\Gamma(0^n)|})=1]|$ over PPT $D$; $\Gamma$ is a PRG iff $\varepsilon_\Gamma$ is negligible (with the stretching and efficiency requirements). $H'$ is polynomial-time (polynomially many applications of a polynomial-time $H$ to strings of polynomial length) and stretches $n$ to $\ell'(n)>n$.

Let $t=\ell'(n)-n$ and for $0\le i\le t$ define the distribution $A_i=H^{t-i}(U_{n+i})$ ($H^j$ = $j$-fold application): $A_0=H'(U_n)$ and $A_t=U_{\ell'(n)}$. Let $D$ be any PPT distinguisher. Then
$$|\Pr[D(A_0)=1]-\Pr[D(A_t)=1]|\le\sum_{i=0}^{t-1}|\Pr[D(A_i)=1]-\Pr[D(A_{i+1})=1]|.$$
For each $i$ define $D_i(y)=D(H^{t-i-1}(y))$ for $y\in\{0,1\}^{n+i+1}$, a PPT algorithm. Then $D(A_i)=D_i(H(U_{n+i}))$ and $D(A_{i+1})=D_i(U_{n+i+1})$, so the $i$-th term is at most $\varepsilon_H(n+i)$. Since $H$ is a PRG, $\varepsilon_H$ is negligible. Given $k$, choose $N$ with $m^{k+c}\varepsilon_H(m)<1$ for all $m\ge N$, where $t\le n^{c}$ for large $n$ ($t$ is polynomial). Then for $n\ge N$: $\varepsilon_{H'}(n)\le\sum_{i<t}\varepsilon_H(n+i)\le n^c\cdot n^{-(k+c)}=n^{-k}$. So $\varepsilon_{H'}$ is negligible, and $H'$ is a PRG. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2016-power-31.title: Randomized encryption
pumac-2016-power-31.body: $E$ is allowed to use randomness (Definition 4.1.1), so two encryptions of the same message under the same key can differ. A fresh encryption $c=E_k(m_b)$ will in general not coincide with the oracle's earlier answers $E_k(m_0)$ or $E_k(m_1)$, so the proposed test gives no information. (The argument only works against deterministic encryption.) $\blacksquare$

pumac-2016-power-32.title: Contrapositive
pumac-2016-power-32.body: By Problem 5.2, computational indistinguishability is equivalent to guessing indistinguishability. Suppose the scheme fails guessing indistinguishability: there is a PPT adversary $A$ and a non-negligible $\epsilon(n)$ with $\Pr[A\text{ wins}]\ge\frac12+\epsilon(n)$. Let $A'$ be the CPA adversary that never queries its oracle and otherwise behaves exactly like $A$. Then $A'$ wins the CPA game with probability $\ge\frac12+\epsilon(n)$, so the scheme is not CPA secure. Taking the contrapositive proves the claim. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2016-power-33.title: GGM hybrid argument
pumac-2016-power-33.body:
$f_k$ is polynomial-time computable ($n$ applications of $H$). View $f_k$ as a depth-$n$ binary tree: the root is labelled $k$, the node reached by $x_1\dots x_i$ has label $\lambda(x_1\dots x_i)\in\{0,1\}^n$, and the children of a node with label $v$ are labelled $H_0(v)$, $H_1(v)$; $f_k(x)=\lambda(x)$.

*Hybrids.* For $0\le i\le n$ let $\Phi_i$ be the random function obtained as follows: pick a uniformly random function $R_i:\{0,1\}^i\to\{0,1\}^n$ (the labels of level $i$) and set $\Phi_i(x)=H_{x_n}(\cdots H_{x_{i+1}}(R_i(x_1\dots x_i))\cdots)$. Then $\Phi_0$ is $f_k$ for a uniform $k$ and $\Phi_n=R_n$ is a uniformly random function $\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}^n$.

Let $D$ be a PPT oracle distinguisher making at most $q=q(n)$ queries ($q$ polynomial). By the triangle inequality it suffices to bound $|\Pr[D^{\Phi_i}=1]-\Pr[D^{\Phi_{i+1}}=1]|$ by $q\cdot\varepsilon_H(n)$, where $\varepsilon_H$ is the (negligible) PRG advantage; then the total advantage is $\le nq\,\varepsilon_H(n)$, which is negligible.

*One level.* $\Phi_{i+1}$ differs from $\Phi_i$ only in that the pair of children $(H_0(R_i(u)),H_1(R_i(u)))=H(R_i(u))$ of every level-$i$ node $u$ is replaced by an independent uniform $2n$-bit string. Along any run of $D$, at most $q$ distinct level-$i$ nodes $u_1,\dots,u_q$ are touched. Define sub-hybrids $\Psi_j$, $0\le j\le q$: the first $j$ distinct level-$i$ nodes touched get a uniform $2n$-bit string as pair of children, later nodes get $H(\text{fresh uniform }n\text{-bit string})$. Then $\Psi_0=\Phi_i$ and $\Psi_q=\Phi_{i+1}$ in distribution, and $\Psi_{j-1},\Psi_j$ differ only for the $j$-th distinct node: a distinguisher $D'$ for $H$ receives a challenge $y\in\{0,1\}^{2n}$ (either $H(U_n)$ or $U_{2n}$), simulates the oracle by lazily sampling all other labels (fresh uniform strings, or $H$ of fresh strings, as prescribed), uses $y$ for the $j$-th distinct level-$i$ node, runs $D$ and outputs its answer. $D'$ is PPT. Hence $|\Pr[D^{\Psi_{j-1}}=1]-\Pr[D^{\Psi_j}=1]|\le\varepsilon_H(n)$ for each $j$ (guessing $j$ in advance costs a factor $q$ at most, which is already accounted for by summing over $j$ instead). Summing over $j\le q$ gives the bound $q\,\varepsilon_H(n)$ for the pair $\Phi_i,\Phi_{i+1}$.

Therefore $|\Pr[D^{f_k}=1]-\Pr[D^R=1]|\le nq\,\varepsilon_H(n)$, negligible. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2016-power-34.title: Feistel structure and Luby–Rackoff
pumac-2016-power-34.body:
**Bijectivity and inverse.** Put $u=x_1\oplus f_{k_1}(x_2)$ and $v=x_2\oplus f_{k_2}(u)$; then $g_k(x)=(u\oplus f_{k_3}(v))\circ v=y_1\circ y_2$. Given $y=y_1\circ y_2$: $v=y_2$, $u=y_1\oplus f_{k_3}(y_2)$, $x_2=v\oplus f_{k_2}(u)$, $x_1=u\oplus f_{k_1}(x_2)$. So $g_k$ is a bijection with a polynomial-time inverse (given $k$). It remains to show $G$ is a PRF (key generation: generate $k_1,k_2,k_3$ with the PRF's generator).

**Step 1: replace $f_{k_i}$ by random functions.** Let $h_1,h_2,h_3$ be independent uniformly random functions $\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}^n$ and let $g^{h}$ be $g$ with $f_{k_i}$ replaced by $h_i$. Consider the hybrids $(f_{k_1},f_{k_2},f_{k_3})\to(h_1,f_{k_2},f_{k_3})\to(h_1,h_2,f_{k_3})\to(h_1,h_2,h_3)$. If a PPT oracle algorithm $D$ distinguishes two consecutive hybrids with advantage $\delta$, the algorithm $D'$ that, given an oracle $\phi$ (either $f_{k_i}$ or a random function), simulates the oracle for $D$ by computing $g$ with $\phi$ in the $i$-th slot, with the already-replaced slots simulated by lazily-sampled random functions and the remaining slots by the known keys, distinguishes $f_{k_i}$ from random with advantage $\delta$. By the PRF property each step has negligible advantage, so $|\Pr[D^{g_k}=1]-\Pr[D^{g^h}=1]|\le3\,\mathrm{neg}(n)$.

**Step 2: $g^h$ vs a random function.** Let $D$ make $q$ queries $x^{(1)},\dots,x^{(q)}$, WLOG distinct (repeated queries get repeated answers in both worlds). Write $x^{(i)}=x_1^{(i)}\circ x_2^{(i)}$, $u_i=x_1^{(i)}\oplus h_1(x_2^{(i)})$, $v_i=x_2^{(i)}\oplus h_2(u_i)$ and output $y^{(i)}=(u_i\oplus h_3(v_i))\circ v_i$.
* *Event $C_1$: $u_i=u_j$ for some $i\ne j$.* If $x_2^{(i)}=x_2^{(j)}$ then $x_1^{(i)}\ne x_1^{(j)}$ and $u_i\ne u_j$ always. If $x_2^{(i)}\ne x_2^{(j)}$, $h_1(x_2^{(i)}),h_1(x_2^{(j)})$ are independent uniform, so $\Pr[u_i=u_j]=2^{-n}$. Hence $\Pr[C_1]\le\binom q22^{-n}$.
* Given $\neg C_1$, the $u_i$ are distinct, so $h_2(u_i)$ are independent uniform and therefore the $v_i$ are independent uniform. *Event $C_2$: $v_i=v_j$ for some $i\ne j$*: $\Pr[C_2\mid\neg C_1]\le\binom q22^{-n}$.
* Given $\neg C_1,\neg C_2$: the $v_i$ are distinct, so the $h_3(v_i)$ are independent uniform, hence $y_1^{(i)}=u_i\oplus h_3(v_i)$ is uniform and independent of everything else, and $y_2^{(i)}=v_i$ is uniform and independent. So the $q$ outputs $y^{(i)}$ are independent uniform $2n$-bit strings, exactly the answers of a random function on distinct queries.
So the statistical distance between the transcripts is at most $q^22^{-n}$.

**Conclusion.** For every PPT $D$ with $q=\mathrm{poly}(n)$ queries, $|\Pr[D^{g_k}=1]-\Pr[D^{R}=1]|\le3\,\mathrm{neg}(n)+q^22^{-n}$, which is negligible ($R$ a random function on $\{0,1\}^{2n}$). So $G$ is a PRF consisting of bijections with efficient inverses: a PRP. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2016-power-35.title: Counter mode
pumac-2016-power-35.body:
**Decryption.** $D_k(VI\circ c_1\circ\dots\circ c_t)$ computes $f_k(VI+i-1)$ and outputs $m_i=c_i\oplus f_k(VI+i-1)$ for each $i$. It is deterministic and polynomial-time, and $D_k(E_k(m))=m$. $E$ is PPT.

**Security.** Let $A$ be a PPT CPA adversary making at most $q=\mathrm{poly}(n)$ encryption queries (including the challenge), each of at most $n$ blocks. A PRP is a PRF, so replacing $f_k$ by a uniformly random function $R:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}^n$ changes the winning probability of $A$ by at most $\mathrm{neg}(n)$ (a distinguisher simulates the whole game, using its oracle for every evaluation of $f_k$, and outputs $1$ iff $A$ wins). So it suffices to show that against a random $R$ the adversary wins with probability at most $\frac12+q^2\cdot2n/2^n$.

*The random-function game.* The $j$-th ciphertext uses the pad blocks $R(VI_j),\dots,R(VI_j+t_j-1)$ with an independent uniform $VI_j$. Let $\mathrm{Bad}$ be the event that two of the intervals $[VI_j,VI_j+t_j-1]\subseteq\mathbb Z/2^n$ intersect. For two ciphertexts $j\ne j'$ the intervals meet iff $VI_{j'}-VI_j\bmod2^n\in(-t_{j'},t_j)$, a set of at most $2n$ residues; as $VI_{j'}$ is uniform and independent of $VI_j$ (and of the adversary's choice of messages, which depend only on earlier ciphertexts' values, not on a not-yet-chosen $VI_{j'}$), this has probability $\le2n/2^n$. A union bound over the $\binom q2$ pairs gives $\Pr[\mathrm{Bad}]\le q^2n/2^n$.

*If Bad does not occur*, all pad blocks used (including those of the challenge ciphertext) are values of $R$ at distinct points, hence independent uniform strings, so every ciphertext block is a uniform string independent of the messages: in particular the challenge ciphertext $c=VI\circ(\text{pads}\oplus m_b)$ is distributed identically for $b=0$ and $b=1$ and independent of the adversary's view. So $A$ guesses $b$ with probability exactly $\frac12$.

Hence $\Pr[A\text{ wins with }R]\le\frac12+\Pr[\mathrm{Bad}]\le\frac12+q^2n/2^n$, and with the real PRP $\Pr[A\text{ wins}]\le\frac12+\mathrm{neg}(n)+q^2n/2^n$, which is $\frac12+$ a negligible function. So $(G,E,D)$ is CPA secure. $\blacksquare$
